# How to Solve a Timeout Error in Laravel 5 When you encounter a `Maximum execution time of 30 seconds exceeded` error, your first instinct might be to assume the database query is simply too slow. In the specific case described in recent reports involving Laravel 5, however, the culprit often lies not in the data retrieval itself, but in the application's response to that data. The stack trace points to `Str::snake()` within `ControllerInspector`, suggesting that the framework is attempting to inspect a route or controller method while processing a massive dataset. The core issue arises from how Laravel handles eager loading and view rendering when dealing with large result sets. In the standard setup, fetching all articles via `$articles = Article::all()` loads every record into memory. If your database contains thousands of rows, this creates a significant memory footprint. While `Article::latest()->get()` technically orders the results, it does not limit the number of records returned unless you explicitly specify a count or paginate. The error manifests because Laravel 5 has a default execution time limit set to 30 seconds. When the view attempts to iterate over a large collectionârendering hundreds of `
` blocks with nested HTMLâthe rendering process can easily exceed this threshold. Furthermore, the stack trace indicates that `ControllerInspector` is being invoked during route processing. This often happens when using dynamic helpers like `action()` inside Blade templates to generate links. If the view loop is excessively heavy, it triggers shutdown hooks or routing introspection logic that runs outside the intended request cycle context or consumes excessive resources, leading to the fatal error before the response is fully sent. To resolve this without simply increasing the timeout (which masks the underlying performance issue), you must address the data volume being processed. The most effective approach is to paginate the results. Instead of loading the entire dataset into memory and rendering it in a single request, divide the content across multiple pages. This drastically reduces memory usage and ensures that the view rendering completes well within the execution time limit. You can implement pagination by modifying your controller method to use `with()` for eager loading if necessary, and then applying `paginate()`: ```php public function index() { $articles = Article::latest()->paginate(15); // Adjust page size as needed return View('articles.index', compact('articles')); } ``` On the frontend, you need to update the view to display only a single page of results and include pagination controls. Laravel provides a `links()` helper that automatically generates standard navigation links: ```blade
@foreach($articles as $article)

{{ $article->title }}

{{ Str::limit($article->body, 100) }}

@endforeach
{{ $articles->links() }} ``` By limiting the output to 15 items per page, the rendering process becomes instantaneous. Additionally, consider using `Str::limit()` on the body text in the view to prevent loading massive amounts of text into the DOM for a single request. If you must display a larger list without pagination, ensure that your database queries are optimized with appropriate indexes on the columns used for sorting and filtering. However, relying on raw execution time limits is rarely the correct architectural solution. If this specific scenario persists after implementing pagination, you may need to adjust the `max_execution_time` setting in your `.htaccess` file or `php.ini`, but only as a last resort. For more details on configuring Laravel 5 environments, refer to the documentation available at https://laravelcompany.com.
